```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr)
  library(tidyr)
  library(purrr)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(scales)
  library(knitr)
  library(posterior)
})

# Shared figure look-and-feel.  Per-figure theme() calls below should
# only add what this default doesn't already cover (e.g., rotating
# x-axis text on a single figure).
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
          theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
                legend.position  = "bottom",
                strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
                axis.title       = element_text(size = 10),
                axis.text        = element_text(size = 9),
                plot.caption     = element_text(size = 8, hjust = 0)))

# Posterior draws from the multiple-imputation fit produced by
# ../code/run_fit_mi.R, which pools M=50 SHASH+Dirichlet fits
# over imputed datasets that resample each named-group's printed band
# percentage uniformly from its rounding interval and derive No
# Response by subtraction from the exact cohort band counts.  Stored
# as 50 per-imputation files (small enough to commit) plus a small
# meta file; we reassemble them in memory here.
.mi_dir    <- "../replicated/sims/mi"
.mi_meta   <- readRDS(file.path(.mi_dir, "meta.rds"))
.imp_files <- sort(list.files(.mi_dir, pattern = "^imp_\\d+\\.rds$",
                              full.names = TRUE))
stopifnot(length(.imp_files) == .mi_meta$M)
.draws_dm  <- as_draws_matrix(
  do.call(rbind, lapply(.imp_files, function(f) readRDS(f)$draws)))
.mi_obj    <- c(list(draws = .draws_dm), .mi_meta)
.n_div_mi  <- .mi_obj$n_div
DRAWS <- list(
  draws = function(variables = NULL, format = "matrix") {
    out <- if (is.null(variables)) .draws_dm
           else subset_draws(.draws_dm, variable = variables, regex = FALSE)
    if (format == "matrix") return(out)
    if (format == "draws_df") return(as_draws_df(out))
    stop("format not supported: ", format)
  },
  summary = function(variables = NULL, ...) {
    out <- if (is.null(variables)) .draws_dm
           else subset_draws(.draws_dm, variable = variables, regex = FALSE)
    summarise_draws(out, ...)
  },
  diagnostic_summary = function() {
    list(num_divergent = .n_div_mi, num_max_treedepth = 0)
  }
)
# Race labels, years, group sizes, printed means, and printed band
# proportions, all read from the CSVs by _inputs.R (which also exposes
# the pooled MI draws).  _headlines.R, sourced below, re-sources it.
source("_inputs.R")
RACES <- .RACES
YEARS <- .YEARS
SD    <- list(N = .N_arr, mu_printed = .mu_arr, p_obs = .p_obs)
# RACES order from the driver: White, Hispanic/Latino, Black/African American,
# Asian, Two or More Races, American Indian/Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian/
# Other Pacific Islander, No Response. Keep RACE_LABEL aligned to it.
stopifnot(identical(RACES, c("White", "Hispanic/Latino", "Black/African American",
                             "Asian", "Two or More Races",
                             "American Indian/Alaska Native",
                             "Native Hawaiian/Other Pacific Islander", "No Response")))
RACE_LABEL <- c("White", "Hispanic/Latino", "Black", "Asian",
                "Two or more", "Am. Indian", "Pacific Isl.", "No response")
BAND_LABEL <- c("400--590", "600--790", "800--990",
                "1000--1190", "1200--1390", "1400--1600")
# SAT total scores come in 10-point steps, so the band cut points sit at
# the mid-gap values (the "400-590"/"600-790" boundary is at 595, not 600).
BAND_EDGE  <- c(595, 795, 995, 1195, 1395)   # interior cut points

# Renormalise the observed band proportions to an exact simplex (as the
# Stan transformed-data block does).
P_OBS <- SD$p_obs
for (r in seq_along(RACES))
  for (y in seq_along(YEARS))
    P_OBS[r, y, ] <- P_OBS[r, y, ] / sum(P_OBS[r, y, ])

# Standard (location-0, scale-1) sinh-arcsinh CDF, and its location-scale form.
shash_F  <- function(x, eps, delta) pnorm(sinh(delta * asinh(x) - eps))
shash_Fs <- function(s, mu, sigma, eps, delta) shash_F((s - mu) / sigma, eps, delta)

# Reportable SAT total scores, and the upper edge of each one's rounding
# bin; the discrete percentile (the College Board's convention) of a pmf
# on this grid: smallest grid score whose cumulative probability >= p.
GRIDX <- seq(400, 1600, by = 10)
GRIDE <- c(GRIDX[-1] - 5, Inf)
qgrid <- function(p, cdf, x) { k <- which(cdf >= p)[1]; if (is.na(k)) x[length(x)] else x[k] }

ai <- match("Asian", RACES)
bi <- match("Black/African American", RACES)
wi <- match("White", RACES)
hi <- match("Hispanic/Latino", RACES)
yH <- match(max(YEARS), YEARS)

# Headline numbers quoted in this manuscript's prose.  Defined in
# _headlines.R, sourced here so the abstract and the body pull from
# one place and cannot drift.
source("_headlines.R")
```

# Abstract {.unnumbered}

The SAT, the college admissions test administered by the
College Board, is taken by about two million students in each U.S.
high school graduating class and is scored from 400 to 1600. For the
graduating class of 2026 the College Board's annual report gives a
cohort mean of `r cohort_mean_h` for `r cohort_n_h` test-takers. The College Board does not
release individual scores, even anonymized. Questions such as "what share of
test-takers scoring 1500 or higher are Black?" and "what is the ratio of Asian to
Black test-takers among those scoring 1500 or higher?" cannot be
answered from the published data. For seven racial/ethnic groups and
each graduating class from 2018 through 2026, the College Board does
publish the percentage of each group's test-takers in six wide score
bands. We
fit a Bayesian hierarchical model to those band percentages. We check the model against the cohort-wide summaries the College
Board does publish: the mean, standard deviation, quartiles, and percentiles. For the class of 2026, we estimate that Black test-takers make up `r blk_1500_med`%
(95% CI `r blk_1500_lo`%--`r blk_1500_hi`%) of those scoring 1500 or
higher. The ratio of Asian to Black test-takers among those scoring 1500 or
higher is `r ab_1500_med` (95% CI `r ab_1500_lo`--`r ab_1500_hi`) to one.
These estimates give policy-makers a baseline for judging whether
colleges and universities are complying with the Supreme Court's
decision in *SFFA v. Harvard*.

# Introduction

The SAT [@lemann1999bigtest; @collegeboard_techmanual] is the most
widely used standardized test for college and university admissions
in the United States. It is taken by about two million students in each
high school graduating class. The College Board, a non-profit
membership organization, owns and administers the test, and the data
used here are its own publications. The total score runs from 400 to 1600 in 10-point steps, and
1600 is the maximum. Total scores on the pre-2005 SAT correlate
around 0.8 with omnibus measures of general cognitive ability
[@freydetterman2004]. Scores also predict academic performance after
high school. In the College Board's national validity study of the
redesigned test, the correlation between the total score and
first-year college grade-point average was 0.32 as observed and 0.51
after correction for range restriction [$n$ = 223,858;
@westrick2019validity; see also @sackettkuncelhezlett2009;
@kuncelhezlett2010; @kobrinpatterson2011]. Selective colleges and
merit-scholarship programs impose explicit or de facto thresholds on
the total score.

Our aim is to measure the size of the differences between
racial/ethnic groups at the high end of the SAT scale. We ask two questions. *What share of students scoring at
least 1500 in a given graduating class are Black?* And *what is the ratio of Asian to Black students among those
scoring at least 1500?* We ask
both at 1550 and 1580 as well, and the Appendix reports every quantity
for every group. For more than fifty
years the debate over affirmative action in the United States has
centered on Black representation at elite institutions. In 2023 the
Supreme Court held, in *Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard*, that
the race-conscious admissions programs at Harvard and the University
of North Carolina were unlawful [@sffa2023]. Whether elite schools
have complied is contested, and the composition of their entering
classes since the ruling is the evidence used to judge it
[@kane2026sffa]. The ratio of Asian to Black students in those classes
is one such measure, but it can be judged only against a baseline. If
a school admitted on the SAT alone, what would its class look like?

The College Board does not release anonymized individual-level
scores. Each year
it publishes the *SAT Suite of Assessments Annual Report: Total
Group*, which we call the Total Group report. For seven racial/ethnic
groups, the report gives the number of test-takers, the mean total
score, and the percentage of the group's test-takers in each of six
wide total-score bands. The report gives no standard deviation or percentiles by group, and
nothing finer than the six bands. The 1500
threshold falls inside the top band, 1400--1600, so the share of a
group above 1500 cannot be read from the report. The 2016 report was the last
to print standard deviations by group, and those were for the section
scores on the old 200--800 scale [@collegeboard_annual2016]. The 2026
report drops the standard deviation of the cohort's total score as
well, while keeping the mean, the quartiles, and the per-group band
table [@collegeboard_annual2026].

Placing every
test-taker at the midpoint of their band gives a rough mean and
standard deviation for each group but says nothing about the shape
inside a band. Fitting a normal curve to the band percentages gives a
shape, but the published percentages for several groups are
asymmetric, and a two-parameter symmetric curve cannot follow them.
We instead fit a four-parameter sinh-arcsinh curve, censored at the
limits of the score scale, to each group's band percentages in each
graduating class from 2018 through 2026. A Dirichlet likelihood
connects the curve to the published proportions, and a hierarchy
pools the shape parameters across groups. Methods gives the details
and the reasons for each choice.

A model fit to six band percentages needs a check against data it
never saw, and for the cohort as a whole the Total Group report
supplies one. Each year it prints the cohort's mean and three quartiles, and
through 2025 its standard deviation, none of which enters the fit. The Validation section shows that the model recovers them, to
within a few points, for every year in which they were published, in
most years within the model's own 95% interval. The College Board's fine-grained SAT
User Percentile table, built from individual scores, gives a third
check [@collegeboard_percentiles2025]. Once the integer rounding of
that table is allowed for, the model's cohort-level curve matches it
throughout the body of the distribution and up to the headline
threshold of 1500, with a mild residual at 1550.

The checks stop at the cohort. No public source provides any
per-group quantity above 1400. The percentile table covers the cohort only, so
how the mass above any threshold divides among groups depends on the
accuracy of our model. Every per-group value above 1400 is therefore
an extrapolation, and the 1550 and 1580 values also lie beyond the
cohort-level check.

The models estimated here describe SAT *test-takers*, not all U.S.
18-year-olds. Admissions and scholarship decisions that turn on an
SAT score concern test-takers, so they are the population that
matters for this analysis. Extending these results to the whole age
cohort would require a separate model of who takes the test.

Data presents the published inputs and Methods the model. Results
reports the
fit, the posterior predictive check, the validation against the
published cohort summaries and the percentile table, and the
sensitivity of the headline to the parametric family and the priors.
The section on the composition of the high-scoring pool answers both
questions. For 2026 the Black share and the Asian-to-Black ratio
among test-takers scoring 1400 or higher follow directly from the
published numbers, since 1400 is a band boundary. At 1500, 1550, and
1580 both lie inside the top band and require the model. The Discussion summarizes the findings
and their limits. The Appendix gives, for every group, the estimated
standard deviations by year, the standardized differences between
group means, the shares and counts above each threshold, and the
sensitivity results.

# Data

The data come from the *SAT Suite of Assessments Annual Report: Total
Group* [@collegeboard_annual2018; @collegeboard_annual2019;
@collegeboard_annual2020; @collegeboard_annual2021;
@collegeboard_annual2022; @collegeboard_annual2023;
@collegeboard_annual2024; @collegeboard_annual2025;
@collegeboard_annual2026] for the graduating classes of 2018 through
2026. The College Board also publishes a
separate annual report for each state. We use only the national
report, which we call the Total Group report. Each report gives, by
race/ethnicity, the number of
test-takers, the mean total score on the 400–1600 scale, and the
percentage of test-takers whose total score falls in each of six
bands. The bands are 400–590, 600–790, 800–990, 1000–1190, 1200–1390,
and 1400–1600. The reports identify seven racial/ethnic categories.
They are White, Black/African American, Hispanic/Latino, Asian, Two
or More Races, American Indian/Alaska Native, and Native
Hawaiian/Other Pacific Islander. The reports also give totals for the
full cohort, which is larger than the sum of the seven because some
test-takers decline to report a category.^[In tables and figures we
shorten the longer labels to "Black", "Two or more", "Am. Indian",
"Pacific Isl.", and "No response", the last for the residual group
described below.] The categories are the College Board's. Since 2015
they have followed the U.S. Department of Education's guidelines for
collecting and reporting race and ethnicity, as each report states in
its front matter. Each category pools groups that the published data
cannot separate. "Asian" covers
East, South, and Southeast Asian ancestries with very different
educational histories in the United States, and "Two or More Races"
is by construction a mixture of populations. The model treats each
published category as a single population because that is the only
level at which data exist.

One change to the test falls inside the study window. In March 2024
U.S. administrations moved from paper to a digital, adaptive format,
so the class of 2024 mixes formats and the classes of 2025 and 2026
are almost entirely digital. The College Board reports digital scores on
the same 400--1600 scale and states that they "have the same meaning"
as paper scores, "so no concordance table will be necessary"
[@collegeboard_digital2022]. We take the published scale at face value, and the change matters
little for our results because every group has its own free mean in
every year, the headline quantities concern the
single 2026 cohort, and the only pooling across years, the per-group
scale trend, is relaxed in a refit reported in the Sensitivity
section.

@tbl-pdf gives the seven per-group rows from the 2026 report, though
not in the report's order. The reports for 2018 through 2025 print
the band percentages as a table. The 2026 report presents them as a
stacked bar chart with only some segments labelled, so we read each
percentage from the width of its segment, which the report draws at a
whole percent. The percentages are rounded to integers, so a group's
six bands need not sum to 100. In the 2026 chart the Hispanic/Latino
and Native Hawaiian/Other Pacific Islander rows are identical. We use
them as printed. One rounded value is zero, for Asian test-takers in the 400--590
band, so the true value is below 0.5%. The report also gives the
number of test-takers and the mean score for an eighth row, "No
Response", made up of test-takers who did not report a race or
ethnicity. It does not print band percentages for that row.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pdf
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "**Per-Group Inputs from the 2026 SAT Suite Annual Report.** Test-takers ($N$), mean total score, and the percentage of each group's test-takers in each of six total-score bands, as printed by the College Board. Band percentages are integers and may not sum to 100 because of rounding. Numbers taken from College Board (2026, pp. 9 and 11)."
raw_pdf <- read.csv(sprintf("../replicated/data/race/augmented/%d.csv", HEADLINE_YEAR), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
NAMED7 <- setdiff(RACES, "No Response")
NAMED7_LABEL <- RACE_LABEL[match(NAMED7, RACES)]
pdf_band <- t(sapply(NAMED7, function(rc) {
  vapply(BAND_LABEL_PLAIN <- c("400-590", "600-790", "800-990",
                               "1000-1190", "1200-1390", "1400-1600"),
         function(bo) raw_pdf$percent[raw_pdf$race == rc &
                                      raw_pdf$score_range == bo],
         numeric(1))
}))
pdf_n <- vapply(NAMED7, function(rc)
  raw_pdf$test_takers[raw_pdf$race == rc & raw_pdf$score_range == "all"],
  numeric(1))
pdf_mu <- vapply(NAMED7, function(rc)
  raw_pdf$mean_total[raw_pdf$race == rc & raw_pdf$score_range == "all"],
  numeric(1))
data.frame(
  Group   = NAMED7_LABEL,
  N       = format(pdf_n, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE),
  Mean    = pdf_mu,
  `400--590`    = pdf_band[, 1],
  `600--790`    = pdf_band[, 2],
  `800--990`    = pdf_band[, 3],
  `1000--1190`  = pdf_band[, 4],
  `1200--1390`  = pdf_band[, 5],
  `1400--1600`  = pdf_band[, 6],
  check.names = FALSE,
  row.names = NULL
) |>
  kable(align = c("l", rep("r", 8)), row.names = FALSE)
```

The printed integer percentages in @tbl-pdf are rounded versions of
unobserved true band proportions, so the model does not treat the
table as fixed.
We therefore draw $M = 50$ datasets of plausible true proportions
consistent with the rounding, fit the model to each, and pool the 50 sets of posterior draws, a
multiple-imputation scheme described further in Methods. In each imputation, each named-group row is drawn
uniformly from the six-cell proportion vectors that sum to one and
lie within their rounding intervals,
$\pi_b \in [(k_b - 0.5)/100, (k_b + 0.5)/100)$, with the lower edge
set to $0$ when $k_b = 0$. In practice we sample five cells
independently and accept the draw only if the sixth also lands in its
interval. The No Response band counts are then derived by subtraction
from the cohort *Total* row, whose band counts the College Board
publishes as exact integers. The pooled posterior therefore reflects
rounding uncertainty as well as the uncertainty the Dirichlet
likelihood captures.

Two further College Board sources are held out for validation and
described in the Validation section. They are the published cohort
summaries, which give the mean and three quartiles each year and the
SD through 2025, and the *SAT User Percentile* tables, which are built from individual
scores in ten-point steps. The Validation section cites each table.

```{r}
#| label: fig-data-trends
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "**Mean Total Score and Band-Midpoint SD by Group, 2018--2026.** The left panel shows the published mean total score. The right panel shows the band-midpoint SD, the standard deviation a group's scores would have if every test-taker in a band scored exactly at that band's midpoint. It places each band's published percentage at the nominal midpoints $500, 700, 900, 1100, 1300, 1500$. The exact 10-point-grid midpoints are $495, 695, 895, 1095, 1295, 1500$. The College Board does not publish per-group SDs, so this is a coarse proxy for each group's SD, not the published cohort SD recovered in Validation. Left panel numbers taken from College Board (2018--2026). Right panel calculated by us from the band percentages in the same reports."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4
MID <- c(500, 700, 900, 1100, 1300, 1500)
trends_mean <- tibble(
  race  = rep(RACE_LABEL, length(YEARS)),
  year  = rep(YEARS, each = length(RACE_LABEL)),
  panel = "Mean total score",
  value = as.vector(SD$mu_printed)
)
band_mid_sd <- sapply(seq_along(YEARS), function(yi) {
  sapply(seq_along(RACES), function(r) {
    p  <- P_OBS[r, yi, ]
    mn <- sum(p * MID)
    sqrt(sum(p * (MID - mn)^2))
  })
})
trends_sd <- tibble(
  race  = rep(RACE_LABEL, length(YEARS)),
  year  = rep(YEARS, each = length(RACE_LABEL)),
  panel = "Band-midpoint SD",
  value = as.vector(band_mid_sd)
)
trends <- bind_rows(trends_mean, trends_sd) |>
  mutate(panel = factor(panel, levels = c("Mean total score", "Band-midpoint SD")),
         race  = factor(race,  levels = RACE_LABEL))
ggplot(trends, aes(year, value, color = race, group = race)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) + geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = YEARS, labels = function(b) substr(as.character(b), 3, 4)) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2", name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Graduating-class year ('18–'26)", y = "Score points")
```

```{r}
#| label: nr-numbers
#| include: false
nri <- match("No Response", RACES)
nr_mu <- SD$mu_printed[nri, ]
nr_mu24 <- nr_mu[match(2024, YEARS)]; nr_mu25 <- nr_mu[match(2025, YEARS)]
nr_mu26 <- nr_mu[match(2026, YEARS)]
nr_jump25 <- nr_mu25 - nr_mu24; nr_jump26 <- nr_mu26 - nr_mu25
nr_sd_rise <- round(band_mid_sd[nri, length(YEARS)] - band_mid_sd[nri, 1])
named_sd_rise <- range(round(band_mid_sd[-nri, length(YEARS)] - band_mid_sd[-nri, 1]))
```

The No Response group behaves differently from the named groups in
@fig-data-trends. Its *mean* drifts gently across 2018--2024, jumps
by `r nr_jump25` points in 2025, from a published `r nr_mu24` to
`r nr_mu25`, and rises another `r nr_jump26` points in 2026, to
`r nr_mu26`. No named group's mean moves by that much in a year. The
model allows this because each group has its own free mean parameter
$\theta_{r,y}$ in each year, with no smoothness imposed across years.
The No Response *standard deviation* rises by about `r nr_sd_rise`
points over the period, in steps in 2020 and 2025, while the named
groups' rise by `r named_sd_rise[1]`--`r named_sd_rise[2]` points. The log-linear scale trend the named groups follow
cannot reproduce that. The model therefore gives No Response a free
scale in each year, outside the named-group hierarchy. The public record cannot say whether this reflects a change in who
declines to report a race or in how the same people identify.

```{r}
#| label: fig-band-composition
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "**Score-Band Composition over Time, by Group.** Each panel shows one racial/ethnic group. Score band runs along the horizontal axis, and the nine bars within each band give the percentage of the group's test-takers in that band, by graduating class from 2018 (darkest) through 2026 (lightest). Numbers taken from College Board (2018--2026). The No Response row was calculated by us by subtraction from the published cohort band counts."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6.5
band_long <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_along(RACES), function(r) {
  purrr::map_dfr(seq_along(YEARS), function(yi) {
    tibble(race    = RACE_LABEL[r],
           year    = factor(YEARS[yi], levels = YEARS),
           band    = BAND_LABEL,
           percent = 100 * P_OBS[r, yi, ])
  })
}) |> mutate(race = factor(race, levels = RACE_LABEL),
             band = factor(band, levels = BAND_LABEL))
ggplot(band_long, aes(band, percent, fill = year)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.9), width = 0.85) +
  facet_wrap(~ race, ncol = 4) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "D", name = "Year") +
  labs(x = "Score band", y = "Percent of group's test-takers") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        legend.key.width = unit(0.6, "lines"),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1, size = 7.5),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 9, face = "bold"))
```

```{r}
#| label: topband-range
#| include: false
.tb <- function(r) {
  v <- 100 * P_OBS[match(r, RACES), , 6]
  lo <- round(min(v)); hi <- round(max(v))
  if (lo == hi) sprintf("%d%%", lo) else sprintf("%d--%d%%", lo, hi)
}
wht_tb <- .tb("White");  asn_tb <- .tb("Asian")
blk_tb <- .tb("Black/African American")
hsp_tb <- .tb("Hispanic/Latino")
```

Two more patterns show in @fig-band-composition. Most named-group
band shares barely change from year to year. The 1400--1600 share
moves by at most four percentage points for every named group. Its range is about `r wht_tb` for White, `r asn_tb` for Asian,
`r blk_tb` for Black, and `r hsp_tb` for Hispanic/Latino test-takers,
and no wider for the smaller groups. For most
bands the nine yearly bars are nearly the same height, which leaves
the year-constant skewness and tail-weight little to fit against. The
1000–1190 band, by contrast, declines steadily for White, Black, and
Hispanic/Latino test-takers. This mirrors the slow fall in those
groups' published means in @fig-data-trends. From 2018 to 2026 the
White mean fell from `r SD$mu_printed[wi, 1]` to
`r SD$mu_printed[wi, yH]`, the Black mean from
`r SD$mu_printed[bi, 1]` to `r SD$mu_printed[bi, yH]`, and the
Hispanic/Latino mean from `r SD$mu_printed[hi, 1]` to
`r SD$mu_printed[hi, yH]`.

# Methods

The model combines a flexible parametric curve for each group's score
distribution, a likelihood that connects the curve to the rounded
band proportions, and a hierarchy that ties the per-group parameters
together.

## A Censored Sinh-Arcsinh Shape {#sec-shape}

For racial/ethnic group $r = 1, \dots, 8$ and graduating-class year
$y$, we model an individual total score $S$ as a sinh-arcsinh, or
SHASH, random variable [@jonespewsey2009]. The SHASH is a
four-parameter generalization of the normal with separate parameters
for asymmetry and tail thickness. It is used within the GAMLSS
framework for modeling individual-level distributions
[@rigbystasinopoulos2005; @stasinopoulosrigby2007]. If
$Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$, the standardized SHASH variable is

$$
X = \sinh(\frac{\operatorname{asinh}(Z) + \epsilon}{\delta}),
\qquad \delta > 0,
$$ {#eq-shash}

and the score is $S = \mu_{r,y} + \sigma_{r,y} X$, with location
$\mu_{r,y}$, scale $\sigma_{r,y}$, skewness $\epsilon_r$, and
tail-weight $\delta_r$. Setting $\epsilon = 0,\, \delta = 1$ recovers the
standard normal, $\delta < 1$ gives heavier tails and $\delta > 1$
lighter. The skewness and tail-weight are group-level and
year-constant, pooled hierarchically. The location is a free
per-(group, year) parameter under a weakly informative prior, with
the published mean playing no part. The scale varies by year through
a per-group log-linear trend plus a small per-cell residual.

The sinh-arcsinh CDF, @eq-cdf below, is closed-form. The likelihood evaluates that CDF at five cut points
per group and year on every HMC leapfrog step, which rules out
families such as Azzalini's skew-t whose CDF needs numerical
integration. The family's skewness and tail-weight parameters act
separately
and can be interpreted separately, which the hierarchical pooling
relies on. The one alternative with a closed-form CDF and both
parameters, the two-piece skew-t of @fernandezsteel1998, was fit as a
check in the Sensitivity section. Its degrees of freedom land near
the normal-tail limit, so it offers no tail flexibility the
sinh-arcsinh lacks.

Because $\sinh$ and $\operatorname{asinh}$ are monotone, the SHASH CDF
is the normal CDF $\Phi$ composed with the inverse transformation,

$$
F(s \mid \mu, \sigma, \epsilon, \delta)
  = \Phi(\sinh(\delta \operatorname{asinh}(\frac{s - \mu}{\sigma}) - \epsilon)).
$$ {#eq-cdf}

Censoring at the reporting range is handled by folding it into the
band boundaries. SAT total scores are reported in 10-point steps, so
the latent cut between bands "400--590" and "600--790" sits at the
midpoint of the gap, 595, and the interior cuts likewise at 795,
995, 1195, 1395. With edges
$(-\infty, 595, 795, 995, 1195, 1395, +\infty)$, the bottom band
collects mass the smooth distribution would place below 400 and the
top band mass above 1600, so the model probability that a member of
group $r$ in year $y$ falls in band $b$ is

$$
\pi_{r,y,b} = F(e_b \mid \mu_{r,y}, \sigma_{r,y}, \epsilon_r, \delta_r)
                 - F(e_{b-1} \mid \mu_{r,y}, \sigma_{r,y}, \epsilon_r, \delta_r),
$$ {#eq-bandprob}

a difference of two closed-form CDF evaluations. The same 10-point
convention applies to thresholds later, so a reported score of at
least $t$ corresponds to a latent score of at least $t-5$. The band data alone do not identify the shape within the top band.^[For the highest-scoring group, Asian test-takers, about 26%
of the mass is in the top band. The censoring fold then implies a
small pile-up at the 1600 ceiling, whose practical consequence is
discussed in the section on the composition of the high-scoring
pool.]

Of the four parameters, only the scale is given time structure. The
published cohort SD rose from approximately 204 to 235 across
2018--2025, the last year it was published. A
model with fixed per-group scales would sit at the all-years
average and be too narrow in recent cohorts. For each of the seven
*named* groups we let

$$
\sigma_{r,y} = \sigma_r \exp(\lambda_r z_y + \eta_{r,y}),
$$ {#eq-scaletrend}

with $\sigma_r$ the mid-period scale, $z_y$ the standardized year,
$\lambda_r$ a per-group log-linear growth rate pooled toward a common
$\beta_\lambda$, and $\eta_{r,y}$ a residual for each group and year.
A tight prior holds the residual near zero, but it is estimated, so
the cohort statistics carry its uncertainty. The fitted
$\beta_\lambda \approx 0.04$ corresponds to scales about 13% wider in
2026 than in 2018.

The eighth group, "No Response", receives a free per-year log scale
instead of the log-linear trend, for the reasons given in Data.

The per-group-year location is a free parameter $\mu_{r,y}$. The
published group mean $\bar S^{\text{pub}}_{r,y}$ is not used in the fit.
It and the band percentages come from the same test-takers, so treating
the mean as a separate exact fact would double-count. Holding it out also turns the published group means into a check,
like the cohort SD and quartiles.

The "Two or More Races" group is fit with the same single SHASH
curve, with one skewness and one tail-weight, as each single-race
group.^[The group is by construction a mixture of distinct
populations. But six band totals per cell cannot identify a richer
mixture density for this one group, and the residuals in
@fig-ppc-resid do not visibly require one.]

## A Dirichlet Likelihood on Band Proportions {#sec-likelihood}

For each group and year, let
$\hat p_{r,y,\bullet} = (\hat p_{r,y,1}, \dots, \hat p_{r,y,6})$ be
the six band proportions for that imputation, each in $[0, 1]$ and
summing to one by construction. We model these *observed proportions
directly*, with no reconstructed counts, as

$$
\hat p_{r,y,\bullet} \sim \text{Dirichlet}(\phi_r \pi_{r,y,\bullet}),
$$ {#eq-dirichlet}

where $\pi_{r,y,\bullet}$ are the SHASH band probabilities of
@eq-bandprob and $\phi_r > 0$ is a per-group concentration parameter,
pooled hierarchically across groups. The Dirichlet has mean
$\pi_{r,y,\bullet}$ and component variances
$\pi_{r,y,b}(1 - \pi_{r,y,b})/(\phi_r + 1)$, which do not depend on
the group size $N_{r,y}$. A small group is therefore not treated as
orders of magnitude noisier than a large one. The per-group
concentration, fit from the data, governs the precision of every
reported proportion.

Group-size invariance matches how the published percentages were
produced. They are *coarsened* in the sense of @heitjan1989,
@heitjanrubin1991, and @heitjan1994, that is, rounded to the nearest
integer percentage point [see also @wangheitjan2008]. That rounding
noise is the same size in percentage points for every group. A
multinomial likelihood on reconstructed counts would instead treat
the largest group's band proportions as about
$\sqrt{N_\text{max}/N_\text{min}} \approx 16$ times more precise than
the smallest group's. In practice it gives only about 13% coverage of
nominal 90% predictive intervals. The Dirichlet decouples dispersion
from $N$ and lets the per-group concentration absorb the remaining
misfit within each group.

Rounding noise is handled outside the Dirichlet by *multiple
imputation* [@rubin1987mi], using the rejection sampler described in
Data. Each named-group row is drawn uniformly from the part of the
simplex that lies inside its rounding box, and No Response is derived
by subtraction from the exact published cohort band counts. The full
model is fit to each of the $M = 50$ imputed datasets, and the
posterior draws are pooled. Printed zeros need no special treatment,
because the imputation samples the rounding interval $[0, 0.5)$
directly.

Pooling draws across imputations has a direct Bayesian reading
[@rubin1987mi; @gelman2013bda, ch. 18]. Write $p$ for the true band
proportions and $k$ for the printed integers. The pooled draws are
then samples from $\int \Pr(\theta \mid p)\, g(p \mid k)\, dp$ with
$g$ uniform on the rounding box. That is the exact posterior for
$\theta$ under the coarse-data model of @heitjanrubin1991 with a
uniform coarsening prior. It differs from the full joint posterior
$\Pr(\theta, p \mid k)$ only in that $g$ does not condition on the
SHASH likelihood, so proportions the model finds implausible are not
down-weighted within the box. Each box is one percentage point wide
and the fitted Dirichlet scatter is about two points, so the
likelihood is nearly flat across a box and the two posteriors are
close. Where they differ, the pooled posterior is wider, so the reported
intervals err on the wide side with respect to rounding.

A single concentration per group forces the wide central bands and
the narrow tail bands to share one dispersion, where the rounding
noise is constant in percentage points and the Dirichlet variance
scales with $\pi(1-\pi)$. The resulting over-coverage in the tail
bands is documented in the posterior predictive check.

## Hierarchical Structure {#sec-hierarchy}

All six per-group parameters are pooled hierarchically in the same
way, each drawn from a Gaussian centered at a cross-group mean. The
smallest groups, Native Hawaiian/Other Pacific Islander and American
Indian/Alaska Native, therefore shrink toward the cross-group average
instead of tracking their own sampling noise, the usual
small-area-estimation logic [@fayherriot1979; @pfeffermann2013;
@raomolina2015] applied to groups rather than areas. The log-scale, the skewness, and the
log-scale growth rate are unconstrained, so they are pooled directly,

$$
\log\sigma_r \sim \mathcal{N}(\beta_\sigma, \tau_\sigma), \qquad
\epsilon_r \sim \mathcal{N}(\beta_\epsilon, \tau_\epsilon), \qquad
\lambda_r \sim \mathcal{N}(\beta_\lambda, \tau_\lambda).
$$ {#eq-hier}

The tail-weight, the Dirichlet concentration, and the scale-residual
SD must be positive, so they are pooled on the log scale,

$$
\log\delta_r \sim \mathcal{N}(\beta_\delta, \tau_\delta), \qquad
\log\phi_r   \sim \mathcal{N}(\beta_\phi,   \tau_\phi),   \qquad
\log\tau_{\eta,r} \sim \mathcal{N}(\beta_{\tau_\eta}, \tau_{\tau_\eta}).
$$ {#eq-hier-extra}

The tail-weights are the parameters the band data identify least
well, since they govern the shape inside the top band, which six
band totals cannot recover. The per-group-year scale residuals
themselves are
$\eta_{r,y} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \tau_{\eta,r})$, year-level
departures from the log-linear scale trend rather than additional
structure. The "No
Response" group's scale is unpooled, as described above. Its skewness
$\epsilon_{\text{NR}}$, tail-weight $\delta_{\text{NR}}$, and
concentration $\phi_{\text{NR}}$ remain in the hierarchies of
@eq-hier and @eq-hier-extra.

## Priors and Estimation {#sec-estimation}

The hyperpriors are weakly informative. For the named-group
hierarchies on the within-group scale, skewness, and scale-growth
rate, each mean has a Gaussian prior and each spread a half-normal
prior,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\beta_\sigma     &\sim \mathcal{N}(\log 230, 0.4),  &\quad
\tau_\sigma      &\sim \mathcal{N}^{+}(0, 0.35), \\
\beta_\epsilon   &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.6),         &\quad
\tau_\epsilon    &\sim \mathcal{N}^{+}(0, 0.8),  \\
\beta_\lambda      &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.15),        &\quad
\tau_\lambda     &\sim \mathcal{N}^{+}(0, 0.06).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-priors-core}

The hierarchies on the tail-weight, Dirichlet concentration, and
scale-residual SD are also weakly informative, and the settings for
$\beta_\delta$ and $\tau_\delta$ center each $\delta_r$ near $1$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\beta_\delta       &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.3),           &\quad
\tau_\delta        &\sim \mathcal{N}^{+}(0, 0.2),  \\
\beta_\phi         &\sim \mathcal{N}(\log 300, 1.5),    &\quad
\tau_\phi          &\sim \mathcal{N}^{+}(0, 0.5),  \\
\beta_{\tau_\eta}  &\sim \mathcal{N}(\log 0.03, 0.6),   &\quad
\tau_{\tau_\eta}   &\sim \mathcal{N}^{+}(0, 0.3).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-priors-aux}

We parameterize the SHASH location $\mu_{r,y}$ by the cell's
*expected score* $\theta_{r,y} = \mathbb{E}[S_{r,y}]$, with prior
$\theta_{r,y} \sim \mathcal{N}(1050, 300)$. This is the *centered
parameterization* from the skew-normal literature [@azzalini1985;
@azzalini2014], which removes a near-singularity in the likelihood,
applied here to the sinh-arcsinh family [@jonespewsey2009]. The raw
location is then
$\mu_{r,y} = \theta_{r,y} - \sigma_{r,y}\,m(\epsilon_r, \delta_r)$,
where $m(\epsilon, \delta) = \mathbb{E}[X]$ is computed by 24-node
Gauss–Hermite quadrature once per group per draw. The prior is
centred near the overall SAT mean and is wide enough to be
essentially flat over plausible group means. The fitted medians run
from about 872 to 1250, all within 0.7 prior SDs of the centre. It matters only for the smallest groups. The No Response group's
free log scale in each year has prior
$\log\sigma_{\text{NR},y} \sim \mathcal{N}(\log 230, 0.4)$,
independent across years. The group-level hierarchy uses the
non-centered parameterization throughout.

The model is fit by Hamiltonian Monte Carlo in Stan
[@carpenter2017stan; @betancourt2017hmc] via cmdstanr [@cmdstanr2024]
in R [@rcore2024], using the *posterior* [@burkner2025posterior],
*dplyr* [@wickham2023dplyr], and *ggplot2* [@wickham2016ggplot2]
packages. Each of the $M = 50$ imputed datasets is fit with two
chains of 1,000 warmup and 1,000 retained iterations at
$\text{adapt\_delta} = 0.95$, giving 100,000 pooled draws. Convergence is assessed with the rank-normalized split-$\widehat R$
and effective sample size [@vehtari2021rhat], and fit with posterior
predictive checks [@rubin1984bayesianly; @meng1994posterior;
@gelman1996ppc; @gelman2013bda] and agreement with held-out
summaries, following @gabryworkflow2019. We report 95% credible
intervals for the headline quantities and 90% intervals for the
per-group parameters. All code and data are available, as described
at the end of the paper.

# Results

## Fit and Identification

```{r}
#| label: diag-summary
#| include: false
# Per-imputation diagnostics aggregated by the MI driver
max_rhat   <- .mi_obj$max_rhat_across_imp
min_bulk   <- .mi_obj$min_ess_bulk_across_imp
min_tail   <- .mi_obj$min_ess_tail_across_imp
n_div      <- .mi_obj$n_div
n_imp      <- .mi_obj$M
iters_per_imp <- nrow(.mi_obj$draws) / n_imp     # ~1,200 (2 chains x 600 samples)
total_iters   <- nrow(.mi_obj$draws)
.pp   <- .mi_obj$per_param_diag
.pp_grp  <- .pp[grepl("^(delta|epsilon)\\[", .pp$variable), ]
.pp_cell <- .pp[grepl("^(mu|sigma_ry)\\[", .pp$variable), ]
rhat_beta_phi <- .pp$rhat[.pp$variable == "beta_log_phi"]
ess_beta_eps  <- .pp$ess_bulk[.pp$variable == "beta_eps_mean"]
```

@tbl-diag gives the convergence diagnostics across imputations.
Raising the HMC adaptation target to $\text{adapt\_delta} = 0.95$
from the cmdstanr default of 0.8 leaves `r n_div` divergent
transitions across the 50 imputations,
`r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * n_div / total_iters)` of pooled iterations.
The worst-case $\widehat R$ and ESS [@vehtari2021rhat] sit slightly
outside the conventional thresholds. The parameters responsible are
two cross-group means, the Dirichlet concentration mean $\beta_\phi$
with $\widehat R = `r sprintf("%.3f", rhat_beta_phi)`$ and the
skewness mean $\beta_\epsilon$ with bulk ESS
`r round(ess_beta_eps)`, each in its worst imputation. The per-group $\delta_r$ and $\epsilon_r$, by contrast, have
$\widehat R \le `r sprintf("%.3f", max(.pp_grp$rhat))`$ and bulk ESS
of at least `r round(min(.pp_grp$ess_bulk))` in every imputation. The
per-cell $\mu_{r,y}$ and $\sigma_{r,y}$ that carry the headline have
$\widehat R \le `r sprintf("%.2f", ceiling(100 * max(.pp_cell$rhat)) / 100)`$
and bulk ESS of at least `r round(min(.pp_cell$ess_bulk))`, with a
median of `r format(round(median(.pp_cell$ess_bulk)), big.mark = ",")`.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-diag
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "**Convergence Diagnostics across Imputations.** Aggregated across the M = 50 imputations. Maximum rank-normalized split-$\\widehat R$ and minimum effective sample sizes are taken over per-imputation values, and divergent transitions are summed. Calculated by us from the fitted model, using data from College Board (2018--2026)."
data.frame(
  Diagnostic = c("Maximum rank-normalized split-$\\widehat R$ across imputations",
                 "Minimum bulk effective sample size across imputations",
                 "Minimum tail effective sample size across imputations",
                 sprintf("Divergent transitions (of %s pooled iterations)",
                         format(total_iters, big.mark = ","))),
  Value = c(sprintf("%.3f", max_rhat),
            format(round(min_bulk), big.mark = ","),
            format(round(min_tail), big.mark = ","),
            format(n_div, big.mark = ",")),
  check.names = FALSE
) |> kable(align = c("l", "r"))
```


```{r}
#| include: false
tau_eta_med <- median(DRAWS$summary("tau_eta")$median)
phi_med     <- median(DRAWS$summary("phi")$median)
delta_med   <- median(DRAWS$summary("delta")$median)
delta_rng   <- range(DRAWS$summary("delta")$median)
```

The posterior median of the common scale-trend rate is
`r round(DRAWS$summary("lambda_mean")$median, 2)`
(90% CI [`r round(DRAWS$summary("lambda_mean")$q5, 2)`, `r round(DRAWS$summary("lambda_mean")$q95, 2)`]),
which makes scales about
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100*(exp(diff(range(as.numeric(scale(YEARS))))*DRAWS$summary("lambda_mean")$median)-1))`
wider in 2026 than in 2018. The per-group rates lie in a narrow band
around it. The residuals for each group and year are small, with
per-group residual SDs clustering near `r round(tau_eta_med, 3)`, or
about `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100*tau_eta_med)`. The per-group Dirichlet
concentrations run around `r round(phi_med)`, which implies a
band-proportion scatter of about
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100*sqrt(0.2*0.8/phi_med))` percentage points. The
imputation has already removed rounding noise, so this scatter is
year-to-year drift in shape that the year-constant skewness and
tail-weight cannot follow.

@tbl-params gives the per-group parameters. Scales range from about
190 to 275 across the seven named groups. The tail-weights cluster
near `r round(delta_med, 2)`, ranging from `r round(delta_rng[1], 3)`
to `r round(delta_rng[2], 3)` across the eight groups, just above
one. The tails are therefore nearly Gaussian for every group, and the
groups differ instead in skewness, which is small but positive for
White test-takers, at about 0.05, slightly negative for Asian
test-takers, whose scores bunch near the 1600 ceiling with a tail
trailing to the left, and about 0.4--0.5 for the lower-mean groups,
which have a dense lower bulk and a thin tail of high scorers. The
scale-growth rates are all small and similar. The groups therefore
differ little in *shape*. The disparities in the high-scoring pool
reported below come mostly from differences in means. Two near-normal curves whose means differ by `r wb_gap_h` points, the
2026 White-Black gap, have similar centers and very different tails. Appendix Table A1 gives the standard deviation of
reported scores that the fitted curves imply for every group and
year. The College Board has not published a standard deviation for
any racial/ethnic group since 2016 [@collegeboard_annual2016].

```{r}
#| label: tbl-params
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "**Per-Group Posterior Parameters for the Seven Named Groups.** Each cell shows the posterior median with the 90% credible interval in brackets. $\\sigma_r$ is the mid-period scale, $\\epsilon_r$ the year-constant skewness, $\\delta_r$ the year-constant tail-weight, and $\\lambda_r$ the scale-growth rate, with $\\sigma_{r,y} = \\sigma_r\\exp(\\lambda_r z_y + \\eta_{r,y})$. The No Response group shares the skewness, tail-weight, and concentration hierarchies, with $\\delta_{\\text{NR}} \\approx 1.12$. Its scale is free in each year rather than set by a $(\\sigma_r, \\lambda_r)$ pair, so it is not shown. Calculated by us from the fitted model, using data from College Board (2018--2026)."
gp <- function(par) {
  s <- DRAWS$summary(par)
  s$ri <- as.integer(sub(paste0("^", par, "\\[(\\d+)\\]$"), "\\1", s$variable))
  s |> arrange(ri)
}
slg <- gp("sigma_log0"); eps <- gp("epsilon"); del <- gp("delta"); lam <- gp("lambda")
nri  <- match("No Response", RACES)
named <- setdiff(seq_along(RACES), nri)
# Avoid negative-zero printing on rounded epsilon ('-0.00') by normalising.
fmt2 <- function(x) sub("^-0\\.00$", "0.00", sprintf("%.2f", x + 0))
fmt3 <- function(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)
cell_int  <- function(med, lo, hi) sprintf("%d [%d, %d]", round(med), round(lo), round(hi))
cell_fmt2 <- function(med, lo, hi) sprintf("%s [%s, %s]", fmt2(med), fmt2(lo), fmt2(hi))
cell_fmt3 <- function(med, lo, hi) sprintf("%s [%s, %s]", fmt3(med), fmt3(lo), fmt3(hi))
out <- data.frame(
  Group               = RACE_LABEL[named],
  `$\\sigma_r$`       = cell_int (exp(slg$median[named]), exp(slg$q5[named]), exp(slg$q95[named])),
  `$\\epsilon_r$`     = cell_fmt2(eps$median[named],     eps$q5[named],     eps$q95[named]),
  `$\\delta_r$`       = cell_fmt3(del$median[named],     del$q5[named],     del$q95[named]),
  `$\\lambda_r$`      = cell_fmt3(lam$median[named],     lam$q5[named],     lam$q95[named]),
  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
kable(out, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"), row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: draw-mats

# Plain numeric matrices (not the draws-matrix class) used by the
# cohort-summary and SAT User Percentile validation chunks below.
plain_mat <- function(v) { m <- DRAWS$draws(v, format = "matrix")
  matrix(as.numeric(m), nrow = nrow(m), dimnames = list(NULL, colnames(m))) }
sigry_d  <- plain_mat("sigma_ry")
eps_d    <- plain_mat("epsilon")
mu_d     <- plain_mat("mu")
thmean_d <- plain_mat("theta_mean")
del_d    <- plain_mat("delta")
nit      <- nrow(sigry_d); set.seed(20260511); keep <- sample.int(nit, 300)
```

## Posterior Predictive Check

If the model is calibrated, about 90% of the observed band
proportions should lie inside their 90% posterior predictive
intervals. We draw replicate proportions
$\tilde p_{r,y,\bullet} \sim \text{Dirichlet}(\phi\,\pi_{r,y,\bullet})$
for each of the $8 \times 9 \times 6 = 432$ cells.

```{r}
#| label: ppc-setup
#| include: false
prep <- DRAWS$summary("p_rep", ~ quantile2(.x, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95))) |>
  mutate(idx = sub("p_rep\\[", "", variable), idx = sub("\\]", "", idx)) |>
  separate(idx, into = c("ri", "yi", "bi2"), sep = ",", convert = TRUE)
BAND_HYPHEN <- c("400-590", "600-790", "800-990", "1000-1190", "1200-1390", "1400-1600")
prep <- prep |>
  mutate(obs     = P_OBS[cbind(ri, yi, bi2)],
         in_ci   = obs >= q5 & obs <= q95,
         sd_post = (q95 - q5) / (2 * 1.645),
         z       = (obs - q50) / pmax(sd_post, 1e-9),
         group   = factor(RACE_LABEL[ri], levels = RACE_LABEL),
         year    = YEARS[yi],
         band    = factor(BAND_HYPHEN[bi2], levels = BAND_HYPHEN))
ppc_n_in <- sum(prep$in_ci); ppc_n_tot <- nrow(prep); ppc_pct <- 100 * mean(prep$in_ci)
agg_resid <- prep |> mutate(N = SD$N[cbind(ri, yi)]) |> group_by(yi, bi2) |>
  summarize(obs = sum(N * obs) / sum(N), fit = sum(N * q50) / sum(N), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(d = abs(obs - fit))
ppc_agg_max <- 100 * max(agg_resid$d)
```

In all, `r ppc_n_in` of the `r ppc_n_tot` cells, or
`r round(ppc_pct, 1)`%, fall inside their interval, against the
nominal 90%. The standardized residuals, observed minus predictive
median divided by predictive SD, have mean `r round(mean(prep$z), 2)`
and SD `r round(sd(prep$z), 2)`, less than the value of one a
calibrated model would produce. The Dirichlet predictive intervals
are therefore *wider* than the residuals warrant, especially in the
upper bands, where the 1400--1600 band's residual SD is about 0.4. A
single concentration per group cannot match both the wide central
bands and the narrow tail bands, and the model errs toward the wide
side. A concentration for each band would tighten the tail-band
intervals. The over-coverage means the model overstates its uncertainty
about the top band and about every quantity derived from it, so the
credible intervals reported below are if anything wider than the
data justify.

Summed over groups, the fitted band proportions agree with the
observed ones to within `r sprintf("%.1f", ppc_agg_max)` percentage
points in every year and band. A bias shared by all groups in a year would show up here even if
each cell passed on its own.
@fig-ppc-resid plots the standardized residual for every group, year,
and band. Most scatter around zero with spread well below one,
consistent with the over-coverage just described.

```{r}
#| label: ppc-breach
#| include: false
.brc <- prep |> filter(abs(z) > 1.645) |> arrange(desc(abs(z)))
brc_n         <- nrow(.brc)
brc_n_named   <- sum(.brc$ri != 8)
brc_n_nr      <- sum(.brc$ri == 8)
brc_named_pos <- sum(.brc$ri != 8 & .brc$z > 0)
brc_named_neg <- sum(.brc$ri != 8 & .brc$z < 0)
brc_z_top1    <- round(.brc$z[1], 1)
brc_z_top2    <- round(.brc$z[2], 1)
```

Of the `r ppc_n_tot` cells, `r brc_n` fall outside the $\pm 1.645$
lines, `r brc_n_named` for named groups and `r brc_n_nr` for No
Response. The named-group breaches are all in the 400--590 band, in
2023 through 2026. For the three highest-mean groups, White, Asian,
and Two or More Races, the printed share of that band is zero and the
model predicts a fraction of a percent. For Hispanic/Latino, Black,
and Native Hawaiian/Other Pacific Islander test-takers in 2025 and
2026 the printed share is 4% or 5% and the model predicts 2% to 3%.
That band moved more than any other after 2023, and the year-constant
skewness cannot follow a change confined to one band. The No Response breaches are
all in the lowest band in 2018 and 2019, and they are the two largest
residuals in the figure, $`r brc_z_top1`$ and $`r brc_z_top2`$. In
those years the observed mass is well above what a smooth curve
fitted to the group's other bands will accept.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ppc-resid
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "**Standardized Posterior-Predictive Residuals by Group and Band.** Each point is one cell, a group in a given year and band. Dashed lines mark $\\pm 1.645$, the Gaussian 90% reference under a calibrated model. The Dirichlet 90% predictive intervals used for the coverage count in the text are asymmetric, so the number of points outside the dashed lines need not equal the number of cells outside those intervals. Color shows the score band. Observed proportions taken from College Board (2018--2026). Predictive intervals calculated by us from the fitted model."
#| fig-width: 8.5
#| fig-height: 4.5
ggplot(prep, aes(group, z, color = band)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-1.645, 1.645), linetype = "dashed", color = "grey55") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey25") +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0,
                                        seed = 20260524),
             alpha = 0.8, size = 1.4) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "standardized residual") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
```


## Validation {#sec-validation}

This section tests the method on the whole cohort, the one
population for which the College Board publishes the quantities the
model predicts. Each annual report through
2025 prints five cohort numbers besides the band breakdown the model
is fit to. They are the mean total score, the
standard deviation, and the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentile scores.
None enters the model, and they differ in how strong a check they
provide. The cohort mean is a weighted average of the band
proportions the model fits, and a model that matches the bands
recovers it almost mechanically, so it is only a consistency check.
The
cohort SD is less tightly constrained, since the per-group scale
trend and residuals can fit it without being pinned by the bands. The
quartiles test the shape of the body of the distribution out of
sample. The bands fix the CDF at the five interior cut points, and
where the published $p_{25}$, $p_{50}$, and $p_{75}$ fall between
them depends on the parametric form. Across 2018--2026 that gives 44
cohort numbers, since the 2026 report omits the SD, and the 27 quartiles are the out-of-sample test.

@fig-cohort-mean-sd compares the mean and SD in score points.
Reported quartile scores lie on the 10-point grid, so for them we
compare ranks instead. @fig-cohort-quartile-ranks shows the model's
posterior rank of each published quartile, which should equal 0.25,
0.50, or 0.75.

```{r}
#| label: cohort-stats-compute
#| include: false
muf <- function(r, y) sprintf("mu[%d,%d]", r, y)
tmf <- function(r, y) sprintf("theta_mean[%d,%d]", r, y)
pub_wide <- read.csv("../replicated/data/moments/cohort.csv") |> filter(year %in% YEARS)
cohort_stats <- map_dfr(seq_along(YEARS), function(yi) {
  w  <- SD$N[, yi] / sum(SD$N[, yi])
  pq <- pub_wide[pub_wide$year == YEARS[yi], ]
  k25 <- match(pq$p25, GRIDX); k50 <- match(pq$p50, GRIDX); k75 <- match(pq$p75, GRIDX)
  map_dfr(keep, function(it) {
    cm  <- sum(w * thmean_d[it, tmf(seq_along(RACES), yi)])
    Fhi <- sapply(seq_along(RACES), function(r)
             shash_F((GRIDE - mu_d[it, muf(r, yi)]) / sigry_d[it, sr(r, yi)], eps_d[it, r], del_d[it, r]))
    pr  <- rbind(Fhi[1, , drop = FALSE], diff(Fhi))
    pg  <- as.numeric(pr %*% w); pg <- pg / sum(pg); m <- sum(GRIDX * pg); cdf <- cumsum(pg)
    tibble(year = YEARS[yi],
           stat = factor(c("mean", "SD", "p25", "p50", "p75"),
                         levels = c("mean", "SD", "p25", "p50", "p75")),
           kind = c("score", "score", "rank", "rank", "rank"),
           value = c(cm, sqrt(sum((GRIDX - m)^2 * pg)), cdf[k25], cdf[k50], cdf[k75]))
  })
})
cohort_band <- cohort_stats |> group_by(year, stat, kind) |>
  summarize(q025 = quantile(value, .025), q50 = median(value), q975 = quantile(value, .975), .groups = "drop")
pub_pts <- bind_rows(
  pub_wide |> transmute(year, stat = "mean", kind = "score", ref = mean),
  pub_wide |> transmute(year, stat = "SD",   kind = "score", ref = sd),
  pub_wide |> transmute(year, stat = "p25",  kind = "rank",  ref = 0.25),
  pub_wide |> transmute(year, stat = "p50",  kind = "rank",  ref = 0.50),
  pub_wide |> transmute(year, stat = "p75",  kind = "rank",  ref = 0.75)) |>
  mutate(stat = factor(stat, levels = c("mean", "SD", "p25", "p50", "p75"))) |>
  filter(!is.na(ref))
covtab <- cohort_band |> inner_join(pub_pts, by = c("year", "stat", "kind")) |>
  mutate(hit = ref >= q025 & ref <= q975)
cov5 <- mean(covtab$hit); cov4 <- mean(covtab$hit[covtab$stat != "mean"]); covM <- sum(covtab$hit[covtab$stat == "mean"])
sd_rows <- covtab |> filter(stat == "SD")
sd_model_first <- round(sd_rows$q50[which.min(sd_rows$year)])
sd_model_last  <- round(sd_rows$q50[which.max(sd_rows$year)])
sd_last_year   <- max(sd_rows$year)
sd_miss_years  <- sd_rows$year[!sd_rows$hit]
# per-cell mean recovery vs the published per-group mean
tm <- DRAWS$summary("theta_mean", ~ quantile2(.x, c(.025, .5, .975)))
ix <- do.call(rbind, strsplit(gsub("theta_mean\\[|\\]", "", tm$variable), ","))
tm$ri <- as.integer(ix[, 1]); tm$yi <- as.integer(ix[, 2]); tm$pub <- SD$mu_printed[cbind(tm$ri, tm$yi)]
named <- tm$ri != match("No Response", RACES)
mn_mad  <- median(abs(tm$q50[named] - tm$pub[named]))
mn_cov  <- round(100 * mean(tm$pub[named] >= tm$q2.5[named] & tm$pub[named] <= tm$q97.5[named]))
nr_maxd <- round(max(abs(tm$q50[!named] - tm$pub[!named])))
```

Locating each curve from the bands alone, the model recovers the
published cohort mean to within a few points every year, and the
group means as well. Across the `r sum(named)` named-group cells the median gap
between recovered and published means is about `r round(mn_mad)`
points, and the published value lies inside the model's 95% interval
in `r mn_cov`% of cells. Only the No Response group falls clearly
outside its interval, by up to `r nr_maxd` points. Its mean is
exactly derivable by subtraction, but its band-proportion fit is
looser because of the volatility shown in @fig-data-trends. The
model's cohort SD rises from about `r sd_model_first` in 2018 to
about `r sd_model_last` in `r sd_last_year`, tracking the published
rise from about 204 to 235. The small residual for each year lets it
follow year-to-year fluctuations, but not entirely. In
`r paste(sd_miss_years, collapse = " and ")` the published SD sits at
the edge of the posterior interval, just outside it. The quartile
ranks are within about a percentage point of nominal in most years.
The largest deviations are about $+2$ points for $p_{25}$ in 2018 and
2026 and about $+1.5$ points for $p_{75}$ in 2025 and 2026,
reflecting the recent right-skew residual. Overall, the published
value lies inside the model's 95% interval in `r round(100 * cov5)`%
of the `r nrow(covtab)` cells. That is `r round(100 * cov4)`% of the
`r sum(covtab$stat != "mean")` SD and quartile cells and `r covM` of
the `r sum(covtab$stat == "mean")` mean cells. The misses are small
and mostly at the interval's edge.

```{r}
#| label: fig-cohort-mean-sd
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "**Held-Out Cross-Check of the Cohort Mean and Standard Deviation.** By graduating-class year. Neither summary was used in fitting. The model was fit only to the six banded percentages for each group and year, and the implied cohort mean and SD are computed as population-weighted moments of the fitted group distributions. The blue line is the posterior median of the model's implied cohort value, and the shaded band is its 95% credible interval. Black points are the College Board's published values. The 2026 report gives no SD, so the SD panel has no 2026 point. Y-axes differ between panels. Black points taken from College Board (2018--2026). Model values calculated by us from the fitted model."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.4
cb_s <- filter(cohort_band, kind == "score")
pp_s <- filter(pub_pts,     kind == "score")
ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(data = cb_s, aes(year, ymin = q025, ymax = q975), fill = "#2c7fb8", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(  data = cb_s, aes(year, q50), color = "#2c7fb8", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point( data = pp_s, aes(year, ref), color = "grey10", size = 1.9) +
  facet_wrap(~ stat, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = YEARS, labels = function(b) substr(as.character(b), 3, 4)) +
  labs(x = "graduating-class year ('18–'26)", y = "score points")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-cohort-quartile-ranks
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "**Held-Out Cross-Check of the Published Cohort Quartile Scores.** By graduating-class year. For each year the College Board reports the scores at the cohort's 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles. We plug each of those scores into the model's posterior cumulative distribution to get the percentile the model assigns to it, its implied rank. A perfectly calibrated model places the published 25th-percentile score at percentile 25, the median at 50, and the 75th-percentile score at 75. The vertical axis shows the implied rank minus the nominal value, so the dashed zero line is perfect agreement. The blue line is the posterior median and the shaded band the 95% credible interval. None of the published quartiles was used in fitting. Published quartile scores taken from College Board (2018--2026). Implied ranks calculated by us from the fitted model."
#| fig-width: 7

TARG <- c(p25 = 25, p50 = 50, p75 = 75)
LBL  <- c(p25 = "25th percentile", p50 = "50th percentile", p75 = "75th percentile")
cb_q <- filter(cohort_band, kind == "rank") |>
  mutate(target   = TARG[as.character(stat)],
         dev_q50  = 100 * q50  - target,
         dev_q025 = 100 * q025 - target,

ggplot(cb_q) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(year, ymin = dev_q025, ymax = dev_q975), fill = "#2c7fb8", alpha = 0.2) +

  scale_x_continuous(breaks = YEARS, labels = function(b) substr(as.character(b), 3, 4)) +
  labs(x = "graduating-class year ('18–'26)",
```
