
```{r}
#| label: validate-compute
#| include: false
WINDOWS <- list(
  "2018-2020" = c(2018, 2019, 2020),
  "2019-2021" = c(2019, 2020, 2021),
  "2021-2023" = c(2021, 2022, 2023),
  "2022-2024" = c(2022, 2023, 2024),
  "2023-2025" = c(2023, 2024, 2025))
multi_validate <- purrr::map_dfr(names(WINDOWS), function(wname) {
  years <- WINDOWS[[wname]]; yj <- match(years, YEARS)
  N_w <- SD$N[, yj]; tot_N <- sum(N_w)
  UP <- read.csv(sprintf("../replicated/data/percentiles/user_group_%s.csv", wname)) |>
    mutate(emp = pmax(0, 1 - user_pct / 100))
  # Rounding band for P(score >= t).  The College Board reports the
  # User Percentile as an integer K under the "at or below" convention,
  # except for the topmost scores where it reports "99+" (encoded in the
  # CSV as 99.5).  An integer K at grid score t-10 means
  # P(<=t-10)*100 in [K-0.5, K+0.5), so P(>=t) in
  # (1 - (K+0.5)/100, 1 - (K-0.5)/100] -- a one-percentage-point band.
  # A half-integer 99.5 at t-10 means P(<=t-10)*100 in [99.5, 100], so
  # P(>=t) in [0, 0.5%] -- a half-percentage-point ONE-SIDED band.
  ug_lookup <- setNames(UP$user_pct, as.character(UP$score))
  is_half <- function(x) abs(x - round(x)) > 0.25
  UP <- UP |> dplyr::mutate(
    pct_below = ug_lookup[as.character(score - 10)],
    pct_below = ifelse(is.na(pct_below), 0, pct_below),
    ug_lo = ifelse(is_half(pct_below),
                   0,
                   pmax(0, 1 - (pct_below + 0.5) / 100)),
    ug_hi = ifelse(is_half(pct_below),
                   pmin(1, 1 - (pct_below      ) / 100),
                   pmin(1, 1 - (pct_below - 0.5) / 100)))
  out <- purrr::map_dfr(UP$score, function(t) {
    vals <- purrr::map_dbl(keep, function(it) {
      tot <- 0
      for (r in seq_along(RACES))
        for (j in seq_along(yj)) {
          yy <- yj[j]
          tot <- tot + N_w[r, j] *
            (1 - shash_F((t - mu_d[it, muf(r, yy)]) / sigry_d[it, sr(r, yy)],
                         eps_d[it, r], del_d[it, r]))
        }
      tot / tot_N
    })
    tibble(score = t,
           q50 = median(vals),
           q5  = quantile(vals, 0.05),
           q95 = quantile(vals, 0.95))
  })
  out |> dplyr::mutate(window = wname) |>
    dplyr::inner_join(UP, by = "score")
})
v1500 <- dplyr::filter(multi_validate, window == "2023-2025", score == 1500)
v_drift <- dplyr::filter(multi_validate, window == "2023-2025", score >= 1550) |>
  dplyr::summarize(lo = min(q50 - ug_hi), hi = max(q50 - ug_hi))
# Median-inside-band coverage across all (window, grid score) cells:
ppc_n_in_val <- sum(multi_validate$q50 >= multi_validate$ug_lo &
                    multi_validate$q50 <= multi_validate$ug_hi)
ppc_n_tot_val <- nrow(multi_validate)

# Exact cohort P(score >= t) at every reported band lower-edge per
# window, from the published band data.  These are five hard
# data-pinned anchor points per window at scores 600, 800, 1000, 1200,
# 1400 (the lower edge of each band after the first).  They carry no
# integer-rounding uncertainty: the per-(race, year) band counts sum
# to the published cohort band counts by construction of the
# imputation.
band_edge_scores <- c(600, 800, 1000, 1200, 1400)
exact_anchors <- purrr::map_dfr(names(WINDOWS), function(wname) {
  yj <- match(WINDOWS[[wname]], YEARS)
  tot_N <- sum(SD$N[, yj])
  band_p <- vapply(seq_len(6), function(b)
    sum(sapply(yj, function(y) sum(SD$N[, y] * P_OBS[, y, b]))) / tot_N,
    numeric(1))
  cum_le_upper_edge <- cumsum(band_p)[1:5]
  tibble(window = wname,
         score  = band_edge_scores,
         p      = 1 - cum_le_upper_edge)
})
```

A second, finer check is independent of the band summaries. The
College Board's *SAT User Percentile* table gives, in 10-point steps,
the cumulative share of test-takers at or below each total score in
the three most recently graduated cohorts pooled. It is built from
individual scores, and we hold it out of the fit.

Below 1400 this comparison tests little. The six band proportions pin
the cohort survival curve at five band boundaries, and any smooth
curve through them tracks those anchors to within rounding. Above 1400
the band data give a single anchor, at the bottom of the top band,
and the SHASH form fills in the rest. The table is the only check on the shape inside that band.

The College Board has published the SAT User Percentile table for
five pooled three-year windows, from 2018–2020 through 2023–2025, with
no table for 2020–2022 [@collegeboard_percentiles2020;
@collegeboard_percentiles2021; @collegeboard_percentiles2023;
@collegeboard_percentiles2024; @collegeboard_percentiles2025]. The
table is replaced each year, so we cite an archived copy of each
window. For the most recent window we compute the
model's implied cohort survival curve by population-weighting the
per-group SHASH curves over the three years, and @fig-validate
compares it with the published table. The table reports an integer
percentile at each 10-point score, so the true
$P(\text{score}\ge t)$ lies in a band one percentage point wide, or
half a point wide at the top scores reported as "99+". Through the body of the
distribution the model's posterior median runs within about one
percentage point of the band, mostly a little below it. The exact
cohort anchors at the band boundaries sit below the table's band by a
similar amount, so that offset reflects a small difference between
the two College Board sources rather than the model. From 1400 to
1500 the median lies inside the band or within 0.2 points of it. For
2023–2025 the model puts `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * v1500$q50)`% (90%
interval `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * v1500$q5)`% to
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * v1500$q95)`%) above 1500, and the table's
band runs from 2.5% to 3.5%. From 1550 upward the model drifts above
the band by about `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * v_drift$lo)` to
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * v_drift$hi)` percentage points, until integer
rounding at the top of the table makes further comparison impossible.
The four earlier windows show the same pattern and are not reproduced
here.

From 1550 upward the model places somewhat *more* cohort mass than
the table does. The cohort-level counts at 1550 and 1580 reported
below are therefore more likely too high than too low.


```{r}
#| label: fig-validate
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "**External Held-Out Validation against the SAT User Percentile Reference, 2023--2025 Pooled Cohort.** Grey rectangles show the range of $P(\\text{score} \\ge t)$ consistent with the integer SAT User Percentile at $t-10$. Each is one percentage point tall, or half a point at the top scores reported as '99+'. The solid blue line is the model's posterior median cohort $P(\\text{score} \\ge t)$, population-weighted across 2023--2025. Black points are the exact cohort survival at the band boundaries 600, 800, 1000, 1200, and 1400. Plots for the four earlier windows look similar and are omitted. Grey bands taken from the College Board's SAT User Percentile table for the 2023--2025 window. Black points calculated by us from the band counts in College Board (2023--2025). Blue line calculated by us from the fitted model."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4
ggplot(dplyr::filter(multi_validate, window == "2023-2025"), aes(x = score)) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = score - 5, xmax = score + 5, ymin = ug_lo, ymax = ug_hi),
            fill = "grey30", color = "grey15", linewidth = 0.15, alpha = 0.55) +
  geom_line(aes(y = q50), color = "#2c7fb8", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(data = dplyr::filter(exact_anchors, window == "2023-2025"),
             aes(x = score, y = p), color = "grey15", size = 1.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(400, 1600, by = 200)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(x = "SAT total threshold", y = "P(score ≥ t)")
```

## Sensitivity to the Parametric Family and Priors {#sec-sensitivity}

The shape within the top band, which the headline quantities depend
on, comes from the parametric form. We therefore ask how much those
quantities move under a different form or under looser priors on the
shape parameters. We refit three variants with the canonical sampler
settings, all to the first of the 50 imputed datasets, so that the
comparison isolates the modeling choice from rounding noise. The
first is the two-piece skew-t of @fernandezsteel1998, the one
alternative family with a closed-form CDF and separate skewness and
tail parameters. Its per-group skewness $\gamma_r$ and degrees of
freedom $\nu_r$ are pooled hierarchically in place of $\epsilon_r$
and $\delta_r$. The second is the canonical model with the
between-group tail-weight hyperprior widened five-fold,
$\tau_\delta \sim \mathcal{N}^{+}(0, 1.0)$ in place of
$\mathcal{N}^{+}(0, 0.2)$. The third is the canonical model with
year-varying skewness,
$\epsilon_{r,y} = \epsilon_r + \tau_{\epsilon\text{-year}}\,\eta^{\epsilon}_{r,y}$,
which relaxes the only restriction across years on the shape
parameters.

```{r}
#| label: sens-compute
#| include: false
SENS_DIR <- "../replicated/sims/sensitivity"
sens_ref <- readRDS("../replicated/sims/mi/imp_01.rds")$draws
sens_fit <- lapply(c(skewt = "skewt", widedelta = "widedelta", epsyear = "epsyear"),
                   function(v) readRDS(file.path(SENS_DIR, paste0(v, ".rds"))))
sens_meta <- readRDS(file.path(SENS_DIR, "meta.rds"))
stopifnot(identical(sens_meta$RACES, RACES), sens_meta$m_ref == 1L)
# Fernandez-Steel two-piece skew-t CDF (matches the Stan implementation).
fs_F <- function(z, g, nu) {
  g2 <- g^2
  ifelse(z <= 0, 2 / (g2 + 1) * pt(z * g, nu),
                 1 / (g2 + 1) + 2 * g2 / (g2 + 1) * (pt(z / g, nu) - 0.5))
}
# P(score >= t) for group r in the headline year from a variant's draws matrix.
sens_p_above <- function(d, variant, t, r) {
  saved <- sprintf("p_above_%d[%d,%d]", t, r, yH)
  if (saved %in% colnames(d)) return(d[, saved])
  m <- d[, sprintf("mu[%d,%d]", r, yH)]; s <- d[, sprintf("sigma_ry[%d,%d]", r, yH)]
  if (variant == "skewt")
    return(1 - fs_F((t - 5 - m) / s, d[, sprintf("gamma_r[%d]", r)], d[, sprintf("nu_r[%d]", r)]))
  e <- if (variant == "epsyear") d[, sprintf("epsilon_ry[%d,%d]", r, yH)]
       else d[, sprintf("epsilon[%d]", r)]
  1 - shash_F((t - 5 - m) / s, e, d[, sprintf("delta[%d]", r)])
}
sens_quant <- function(d, variant) {
  cts <- function(t) sapply(seq_along(RACES), function(r) SD$N[r, yH] * sens_p_above(d, variant, t, r))
  fmt_ci <- function(x, dig = 1) sprintf(paste0("%.", dig, "f [%.", dig, "f, %.", dig, "f]"),
                                          median(x), quantile(x, .025), quantile(x, .975))
  c1500 <- cts(1500); c1550 <- cts(1550); c1580 <- cts(1580)
  blk <- function(cc) 100 * cc[, bi] / rowSums(cc)
  c(`Black share of 1500+ (%)` = fmt_ci(blk(c1500)),
    `Black share of 1550+ (%)` = fmt_ci(blk(c1550)),
    `Black share of 1580+ (%)` = fmt_ci(blk(c1580)),
    `Asian/Black ratio, 1500+` = fmt_ci(c1500[, ai] / c1500[, bi], 0))
}
sens_rows <- rbind(
  `Canonical sinh-arcsinh`      = sens_quant(sens_ref, "shash"),
  `Two-piece skew-t`            = sens_quant(sens_fit$skewt$draws, "skewt"),
  `Wide tail-weight prior`      = sens_quant(sens_fit$widedelta$draws, "widedelta"),
  `Year-varying skewness`       = sens_quant(sens_fit$epsyear$draws, "epsyear"))
sens_tab <- data.frame(Model = rownames(sens_rows), sens_rows, check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
# Headline medians for the prose
sens_med <- function(variant, t) {
  d <- if (variant == "shash") sens_ref else sens_fit[[variant]]$draws
  cc <- sapply(seq_along(RACES), function(r) SD$N[r, yH] * sens_p_above(d, variant, t, r))
  median(100 * cc[, bi] / rowSums(cc))
}
sens_range_1500 <- range(sapply(c("shash", "skewt", "widedelta", "epsyear"), sens_med, t = 1500))
sens_range_1580 <- range(sapply(c("shash", "skewt", "widedelta", "epsyear"), sens_med, t = 1580))
nu_med <- sapply(seq_along(RACES), function(r) median(sens_fit$skewt$draws[, sprintf("nu_r[%d]", r)]))
tau_eps_year_med <- median(sens_fit$epsyear$draws[, "tau_eps_year"])
tau_delta_wide   <- median(sens_fit$widedelta$draws[, "tau_log_delta"])
sens_div <- sapply(sens_fit, function(f) sum(f$diag$num_divergent))
sens_rhat <- sapply(sens_fit, function(f) max(f$summary$rhat, na.rm = TRUE))
# Canonical vs skew-t shift at 1500 on the shared imputation, and the
# spread of the canonical per-imputation medians across all 50
# imputations (a like-for-like measure of rounding uncertainty).
sens_shift_1500 <- sens_med("skewt", 1500) - sens_med("shash", 1500)
sens_ci_width_1500 <- {
  cc <- sapply(seq_along(RACES), function(r) SD$N[r, yH] * sens_p_above(sens_ref, "shash", 1500, r))
  x <- 100 * cc[, bi] / rowSums(cc); diff(quantile(x, c(.025, .975)))
}
imp_meds <- sapply(seq_len(.mi_meta$M), function(m) {
  rows <- ((m - 1) * 2000 + 1):(m * 2000)
  cc <- sapply(seq_along(RACES), function(r)
    SD$N[r, yH] * .draws_dm[rows, sprintf("p_above_1500[%d,%d]", r, yH)])
  median(100 * cc[, bi] / rowSums(cc))
})
imp_med_range <- range(imp_meds)
```

@tbl-sens reports the results. Across the four fits, the posterior
median of the 2026 Black share of the 1500+ pool ranges from
`r sprintf("%.2f", sens_range_1500[1])`% to
`r sprintf("%.2f", sens_range_1500[2])`%, and at 1580 from
`r sprintf("%.2f", sens_range_1580[1])`% to
`r sprintf("%.2f", sens_range_1580[2])`%. Every variant's median lies
inside every other variant's 95% interval. The two prior variants
leave every quantity unchanged to two decimals. Under the widened
hyperprior the per-group $\delta_r$ stay clustered, with a fitted
between-group spread of `r sprintf("%.3f", tau_delta_wide)` on the
log scale, so the data rather than the prior produce the cluster near
`r round(delta_med, 2)`. The year-varying skewness term shrinks toward zero, with a
posterior median for $\tau_{\epsilon\text{-year}}$ of
`r sprintf("%.3f", tau_eps_year_med)`. The skew-t is the only variant that moves the headline, raising the
1500 median by about
`r sprintf("%.2f", sens_shift_1500)` percentage points, about
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * sens_shift_1500 / sens_med("shash", 1500))`
of the canonical median and
`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * sens_shift_1500 / sens_ci_width_1500)`% of
the canonical interval's width, and its 1550 and 1580 medians rise by
a similar proportion. Its fitted degrees of freedom are large for
every group, with posterior medians from `r round(min(nu_med))` to
`r round(max(nu_med))`. That is the normal-tail limit of the family,
so the two families agree on the tails and differ only in how their
skewness parameters shape the upper tail. All three variants sampled
cleanly, with at most `r max(sens_div)` divergent transitions in any fit and a maximum $\widehat R$ of `r sprintf("%.3f", max(sens_rhat))`.

The canonical row of @tbl-sens uses a single imputation, so its
median of `r sprintf("%.2f", sens_med("shash", 1500))`%
differs from the pooled headline of `r blk_1500_med`%. Across the 50
imputations the canonical medians run from
`r sprintf("%.2f", imp_med_range[1])`% to
`r sprintf("%.2f", imp_med_range[2])`%. Integer rounding of the
published percentages therefore moves the headline more than the
choice of tail family does, and the pooled interval already includes
that rounding uncertainty. The single-imputation fits in @tbl-sens
omit rounding uncertainty, so their intervals are narrower than those
reported elsewhere. Every variant is also a smooth unimodal curve, so
a family with a separate bump near the ceiling could differ from all
of them above 1550 with no public data to tell them apart. Within the
class of smooth curves, the structural uncertainty in the headline is
small relative to the pooled interval. Appendix Table A4 gives every
group's share of the 1500+ and 1580+ pools under each of the four
fits.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sens
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "**Headline Quantities under Alternative Model Specifications, 2026.** Each cell is the posterior median with the 95% credible interval in brackets, from a fit to the first of the 50 imputed datasets. The canonical row is the canonical model fit to that same imputation, so the four rows are directly comparable. The intervals omit rounding uncertainty and are narrower than the pooled intervals elsewhere in the paper. Every per-group quantity above 1400 is an extrapolation, and 1550 and 1580 also lie beyond the cohort-level check at 1500. Calculated by us from the fitted models, using data from College Board (2018--2026)."
kable(sens_tab, align = c("l", rep("r", ncol(sens_tab) - 1)), row.names = FALSE)
```

# Composition of the High-Scoring Pool

```{r}
#| label: snap-compute
#| include: false
# Posterior quantities for fig-snapshot AND the inline numbers in the
# Applications prose below.  Defined here (before any prose refers to
# it) so that every number in this section -- in the text, the figure,
# and the caption -- pulls from the same posterior draws.
THR <- c(1400, 1500, 1550, 1580)
QLAB <- c(ratio = "Asian / Black ratio", share = "Black share of above-threshold pool (%)")
n_above_1400 <- SD$N[, yH] * P_OBS[, yH, 6]
snap <- map_dfr(THR, function(t) {
  if (t == 1400) {
    rr <- n_above_1400[ai] / n_above_1400[bi]
    pb <- 100 * n_above_1400[bi] / sum(n_above_1400)
    tibble(threshold = t, quantity = c("ratio", "share"),
           q50 = c(rr, pb), q025 = NA_real_, q975 = NA_real_)
  } else {
    # p_above_mat() (from _headlines.R) uses the Stan-saved survival
    # for 1500 and 1550 and evaluates the SHASH survival from the
    # per-cell draws for 1580; the two agree to machine precision
    # where both exist.
    counts <- sweep(p_above_mat(t), 2, SD$N[, yH], `*`)
    rr <- counts[, ai] / counts[, bi]
    pb <- 100 * counts[, bi] / rowSums(counts)
    tibble(threshold = rep(t, 2), quantity = c("ratio", "share"),
           q50  = c(median(rr), median(pb)),
           q025 = c(quantile(rr, .025), quantile(pb, .025)),
           q975 = c(quantile(rr, .975), quantile(pb, .975)))
  }
})
# Inline helpers used by the prose below.  Round so the rendered text
# reads like the figure (one decimal place for percentages, integer
# for ratios).
sg <- function(t, q, col = "q50") snap[snap$threshold == t & snap$quantity == q, col, drop = TRUE]
r1400 <- round(sg(1400, "ratio"))
p1400 <- round(sg(1400, "share"), 1)
```

@tbl-tail gives the estimated share and number of 2026 test-takers
scoring at or above 1500, 1550, and 1580, for the whole cohort and
for the Asian, White, and Black groups. Appendix Table A3 gives the
same quantities, and each group's share of the pool, for all eight
groups. @fig-snapshot shows the
Asian-to-Black ratio and the Black share of the pool above each
threshold, and also at the 1400 band boundary. At 1400 the values
follow directly from the published numbers, subject to their integer
rounding of $\pm 0.5$ percentage points, which matters when the
printed share is itself near 1%. The ratio of Asian to Black test-takers above 1400 is about
`r r1400` to one, and Black students are about `r p1400`% of that
pool. The three higher thresholds fall
inside the top band, where the model interpolates. The Asian-to-Black ratio rises
from about `r ab_1500_med` to one at 1500 (95% CI `r ab_1500_lo` to
`r ab_1500_hi`) to about `r ab_1550_med` at 1550 (`r ab_1550_lo` to
`r ab_1550_hi`) and `r ab_1580_med` at 1580 (`r ab_1580_lo` to
`r ab_1580_hi`). The intervals widen faster than the medians because the rounding
uncertainty in the inputs grows in relative terms as the thresholds
rise.

The No Response group is
`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * SD$N[match("No Response", RACES), yH] / sum(SD$N[, yH]))`%
of 2026 test-takers. Because its 2026 distribution is wide, the model
puts it at about `r nr_1500_pct`% of the pool above 1500. Every share
in @tbl-tail and @fig-snapshot uses all eight groups as the
denominator. If test-takers who declined to report a race differ in
composition from those who did, the named-group shares are diluted
unevenly, and the data cannot say by how much. Using only test-takers
who reported a race as the denominator gives a 2026 Black share of
the 1500+ pool of `r blk_1500_named_med`% (95% CI
`r blk_1500_named_lo`% to `r blk_1500_named_hi`%). The headline lies between these two figures, and the Asian-to-Black
ratio is the same under either denominator.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-tail
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "**Share and Number of 2026 Test-Takers Scoring at or above Three Thresholds.** For the whole cohort and for three groups, the percentage of the group's test-takers at or above each threshold and the implied count. Each entry is a posterior median with the 95% credible interval in brackets. All three thresholds lie inside the top band, so every per-group value is an extrapolation beyond the last point checked by group, 1400. The cohort total is externally checked through 1500 but not at 1550 or 1580. Calculated by us from the fitted model, using the test-taker counts and band percentages in College Board (2026, pp. 9 and 11)."
# Threshold labels go in bold rows inside the Group column rather than
# in their own column, which Word renders too narrow (see Appendix A3).
tail_show <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(1500, 1550, 1580), function(t) {
  rows <- tail_tab[tail_tab$threshold == t, ]
  data.frame(
    Group = c(sprintf("**At or above %d**", t),
              ifelse(rows$group == "Cohort", "Whole cohort", rows$group)),
    `Share of group at or above (%)` =
      c("", sprintf("%s [%s, %s]", rows$pct_med, rows$pct_lo, rows$pct_hi)),
    `Number at or above` =
      c("", sprintf("%s [%s, %s]", rows$n_med, rows$n_lo, rows$n_hi)),
    check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
}))
kable(tail_show, align = c("l", "r", "r"), row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-snapshot
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "**Principal Tail Quantities for the 2026 Graduating Class.** The left panel shows the Asian-to-Black ratio of test-takers at or above each threshold. The right panel shows the Black share of all test-takers above each threshold. At 1400 the values follow directly from the College Board's published numbers and have no credible interval. Their only uncertainty is the $\\pm 0.5$ percentage-point rounding of each group's share of the 1400--1600 band, discussed in the text. The three higher thresholds fall inside the top band, where the model interpolates. Points are posterior medians and bars are 95% credible intervals. All values above 1400 are extrapolations beyond the last point checked by group, and the 1550 and 1580 values also lie beyond the cohort-level check at 1500. The 1400 values are taken from College Board (2026, pp. 9 and 11). The rest are calculated by us from the fitted model."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 3.8
snap$quantity <- factor(QLAB[snap$quantity], levels = QLAB)
ggplot(snap, aes(x = threshold, y = q50)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = q025, ymax = q975), width = 14, linewidth = 0.6,
                color = "#2c7fb8", na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_point(size = 2.1, color = "#2c7fb8") +
  facet_wrap(~quantity, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = THR) +
  labs(x = "SAT total threshold", y = NULL)
```

# Discussion

The 2026 graduating class contained `r cohort_n_h` SAT test-takers,
with a published mean total score of `r cohort_mean_h`, taken from the
College Board's annual report, which for the first time gives no
standard deviation. The published 2026 means were `r mean_h_asian` for Asian,
`r mean_h_white` for White, and `r mean_h_black` for Black
test-takers. From the fitted model,
about `r tq(1500, "Cohort", "pct_med")`% of the cohort, roughly
`r tq(1500, "Cohort", "n_med")` test-takers, scored 1500 or higher.
The corresponding figures are `r tq(1500, "Asian", "pct_med")`% and
about `r tq(1500, "Asian", "n_med")` for the Asian group and
`r tq(1500, "White", "pct_med")`% and about
`r tq(1500, "White", "n_med")` for the White group. For the Black
group they are `r tq(1500, "Black", "pct_med")`% and about
`r tq(1500, "Black", "n_med")`. As a share of the 1500+ pool, Black
test-takers are between `r blk_1500_lo`% and `r blk_1500_hi`%
(posterior median `r blk_1500_med`%), and the ratio of Asian to Black test-takers in that pool is about
`r ab_1500_med` (`r ab_1500_lo` to `r ab_1500_hi`) to one. At 1550 the model puts about
`r tq(1550, "Cohort", "pct_med")`% of the cohort, or
`r tq(1550, "Cohort", "n_med")` test-takers, at or above the
threshold. The Asian, White, and Black counts are about
`r tq(1550, "Asian", "n_med")`, `r tq(1550, "White", "n_med")`, and
`r tq(1550, "Black", "n_med")`. @tbl-tail gives the 1580 figures and
every interval. All of these counts are of test-takers.

We do not convert scores, gaps, or thresholds to IQ equivalents. No
concordance between the current SAT, in use since 2016, and any IQ
test has been published. A conversion based on the test-taker mean
and SD would also look like a population IQ even though test-takers
are a self-selected half of the age cohort. That is the step from test-takers to the age cohort that we do not
take. A standardized gap, Cohen's $d$ against the cohort SD, does
not need that assumption. Appendix Table A2 gives it for every pair
of groups in 2026.

The sinh-arcsinh family [@jonespewsey2009] is well established for
modeling individual-level distributions, principally within GAMLSS
[@rigbystasinopoulos2005; @stasinopoulosrigby2007]. To our knowledge
it has not been fit to banded score data with a Dirichlet likelihood,
and no one has fit a full parametric score distribution for each
group and year from the College Board's public banded summaries.
Published work on group differences in SAT performance has either
relied on individual scores [e.g. @sackettkuncelhezlett2009;
@kuncelhezlett2010; @kobrinpatterson2011] or stayed at the level of
published moments [e.g. @roth2001ethnic; @hauser2002]. The literature
on inferring gaps from coarse public data [@reardon2011;
@reardonkalogridesshores2019] has not paired a parametric
within-group distribution with a likelihood on the proportions
themselves.

The SHASH form interpolates the shape within the 1400--1600 band that
the band data cannot identify. A credible interval from a single
model does not include uncertainty about the model itself. The
Sensitivity section shows that an alternative tail family, a
five-fold wider tail-weight prior, and year-varying skewness move the
headline medians by less than the width of the canonical interval.
Every variant is a smooth unimodal curve, however, so the check
cannot rule out shapes outside that class. Each published
category also pools groups the data cannot separate, so the Asian and
Two or More Races estimates describe the published category, not any
population within it. The Two or More Races group is also, by
construction, a mixture fit with a single smooth curve. The No Response category also appears in every denominator, so the
named-group shares depend on its unknown composition. The Composition
section gives the range.

All of this modeling is necessary only because of how the data are
published. The College Board holds the individual scores from which
every quantity in this paper could be read off directly. It
publishes, per group, six integer-rounded percentages, and its 2026
report no longer prints even the cohort's standard deviation
[@collegeboard_annual2026]. Counts by
group in 50-point bins would make this model unnecessary, as would a
per-group version of the SAT User Percentile table the College Board
already publishes for the cohort. Either would answer both of this paper's questions exactly. The same model can be fit to
any testing report that publishes per-group banded distributions,
such as the ACT or PISA, with whatever other summaries the report
publishes held out as checks, as the cohort SD and quartiles are
here.

# Data and Code Availability

The College Board reports used here are public. They are the Total
Group annual reports for 2018 through 2026 and the SAT User
Percentile tables for the five windows cited in Validation. Copies of
those files, the extraction
scripts, the cleaned data, the Stan model, and the code that produced
every table and figure in this paper are in a public repository at
<https://github.com/davidkane9/sat-total-scores>.

# Appendix {.unnumbered}

The main text reports several quantities for the cohort or for the
Asian, White, and Black groups only. The four tables here give the
same quantities for all eight groups. Every number comes from the same
posterior draws, or the same published figures, as the main text.

## Estimated Standard Deviations by Group and Year {.unnumbered}

The College Board has not printed a standard deviation for any
racial/ethnic group since 2016. Appendix Table A1 gives the standard
deviation of reported scores on the 400--1600 grid that the fitted
curve implies for each group and year, with the model's cohort SD and
the published cohort SD for comparison. The cohort rows are the
quantities plotted in @fig-cohort-mean-sd.

```{r}
#| label: appendix-a1
#| echo: false
set.seed(20261101)
keepA <- sample.int(nit, 2000)
grid_sd <- function(it, r, y) {
  Fhi <- shash_F((GRIDE - mu_d[it, muf(r, y)]) / sigry_d[it, sr(r, y)],
                 eps_d[it, r], del_d[it, r])
  pg <- c(Fhi[1], diff(Fhi)); pg <- pg / sum(pg)
  m <- sum(GRIDX * pg)
  sqrt(sum((GRIDX - m)^2 * pg))
}
a1_cell <- function(x) sprintf("%d [%d, %d]", round(median(x)),
                               round(quantile(x, .025)), round(quantile(x, .975)))
a1_group <- t(sapply(seq_along(RACES), function(r)
  vapply(seq_along(YEARS), function(y)
    a1_cell(vapply(keepA, function(it) grid_sd(it, r, y), numeric(1))),
    character(1))))
coh_sd_draws <- function(y) {
  w <- SD$N[, y] / sum(SD$N[, y])
  vapply(keepA, function(it) {
    Fhi <- sapply(seq_along(RACES), function(r)
      shash_F((GRIDE - mu_d[it, muf(r, y)]) / sigry_d[it, sr(r, y)],
              eps_d[it, r], del_d[it, r]))
    pr <- rbind(Fhi[1, , drop = FALSE], diff(Fhi))
    pg <- as.numeric(pr %*% w); pg <- pg / sum(pg)
    m <- sum(GRIDX * pg); sqrt(sum((GRIDX - m)^2 * pg))
  }, numeric(1))
}
a1_coh <- vapply(seq_along(YEARS), function(y) a1_cell(coh_sd_draws(y)), character(1))
coh_sd_model_h <- round(median(coh_sd_draws(yH)))
a1_pub <- pub_wide$sd[match(YEARS, pub_wide$year)]
a1_pub <- ifelse(is.na(a1_pub), "", as.character(a1_pub))
a1 <- data.frame(Group = c(RACE_LABEL, "Cohort, model", "Cohort, published"),
                 rbind(a1_group, a1_coh, a1_pub),
                 check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
names(a1)[-1] <- as.character(YEARS)
kable(a1[, c("Group", as.character(YEARS[1:3]))], align = c("l", rep("r", 3)), row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "**Appendix Table A1. Estimated Standard Deviation of Total Scores by Group and Year, 2018--2020.** Each cell is the posterior median with the 95% credible interval in brackets, in score points, for the distribution of reported scores on the 400--1600 grid implied by the fitted curve. The model cohort row is the population-weighted mixture of the eight group curves. The College Board publishes no per-group SD. Published cohort SDs taken from College Board (2018--2020). All other values calculated by us from the fitted model.")
```

```{r}
#| label: appendix-a1b
#| echo: false
kable(a1[, c("Group", as.character(YEARS[4:6]))], align = c("l", rep("r", 3)), row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "**Appendix Table A1, continued. Estimated Standard Deviation of Total Scores by Group and Year, 2021--2023.** Layout and sources as in the first part of the table. Published cohort SDs taken from College Board (2021--2023). All other values calculated by us from the fitted model.")
```

```{r}

#| echo: false

      caption = "**Appendix Table A1, continued. Estimated Standard Deviation of Total Scores by Group and Year, 2024--2026.** Layout and sources as in the first part of the table. The 2026 report gives no cohort SD. Published cohort SDs taken from College Board (2024--2025). All other values calculated by us from the fitted model.")
```

## Standardized Differences Between Group Means {.unnumbered}

Appendix Table A2 gives Cohen's $d$ for every pair of groups in 2026,
computed from the published group means and the model's estimate of
the 2026 cohort SD, `r coh_sd_model_h`, from Appendix Table A1. The
College Board published a cohort SD through 2025, and the model's
estimate for each of those years is within a few points of it. We use
the cohort SD as the denominator, rather than a pooled within-group
SD, so that every pair is on one scale. The
Discussion explains why we report standardized gaps rather than IQ
equivalents.

```{r}
#| label: appendix-a2
#| echo: false
ord   <- order(SD$mu_printed[, yH], decreasing = TRUE)
mu25  <- SD$mu_printed[ord, yH]
lab25 <- RACE_LABEL[ord]
pairs <- expand.grid(i = seq_along(ord), j = seq_along(ord))
pairs <- pairs[pairs$i < pairs$j, ]
pairs <- pairs[order(pairs$i, pairs$j), ]
a2 <- data.frame(`Higher-mean group` = lab25[pairs$i],
                 `Lower-mean group`  = lab25[pairs$j],
                 `Difference in means` = mu25[pairs$i] - mu25[pairs$j],
                 `Cohen's $d$` = sprintf("%.2f", (mu25[pairs$i] - mu25[pairs$j]) / coh_sd_model_h),
                 check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
kable(a2, align = c("l", "l", "r", "r"), row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "**Appendix Table A2. Cohen's $d$ Between Published Group Means, 2026.** One row per pair of groups, the higher-mean group first, with groups ordered by mean. The difference in published means, in score points, is divided by the model's estimated 2026 cohort SD. Means taken from College Board (2026, p. 9). SD and $d$ calculated by us from the fitted model.")
```

## Shares and Counts above Each Threshold, All Groups {.unnumbered}

Appendix Table A3 extends @tbl-tail to all eight groups and adds each
group's share of the pool at or above each threshold. At 1400 the
values follow from the published band percentages, subject to their
integer rounding, and carry no model interval. At the three higher
thresholds they come from the pooled posterior.

```{r}
#| label: appendix-a3
#| echo: false
fmtn <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)
a3_pct <- function(x, dig = 1) sprintf(paste0("%.", dig, "f [%.", dig, "f, %.", dig, "f]"),
                                       median(x), quantile(x, .025), quantile(x, .975))
a3_n   <- function(x) sprintf("%s [%s, %s]", fmtn(median(x)),
                              fmtn(quantile(x, .025)), fmtn(quantile(x, .975)))
N25 <- SD$N[, yH]
a3 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(1400, 1500, 1550, 1580), function(t) {
  if (t == 1400) {
    cnt  <- N25 * P_OBS[, yH, 6]
    data.frame(Group = c("**At or above 1400**", "Cohort", RACE_LABEL),
               `Share of group (%)` = c("", sprintf("%.1f", 100 * c(sum(cnt) / sum(N25), cnt / N25))),
               Number = c("", fmtn(c(sum(cnt), cnt))),
               `Share of pool (%)` = c("", "100", sprintf("%.2f", 100 * cnt / sum(cnt))),
               check.names = FALSE)
  } else {
    cnt <- sweep(p_above_mat(t), 2, N25, `*`)
    tot <- rowSums(cnt)
    data.frame(Group = c(sprintf("**At or above %d**", t),
                         "Cohort", RACE_LABEL),
               `Share of group (%)` = c("", a3_pct(100 * tot / sum(N25)),
                 sapply(seq_along(RACES), function(r) a3_pct(100 * cnt[, r] / N25[r]))),
               Number = c("", a3_n(tot), sapply(seq_along(RACES), function(r) a3_n(cnt[, r]))),
               `Share of pool (%)` = c("", "100",
                 sapply(seq_along(RACES), function(r) a3_pct(100 * cnt[, r] / tot, 2))),
               check.names = FALSE)
  }
}))
kable(a3, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"), row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "**Appendix Table A3. Share of Each Group Scoring at or above Four Thresholds, Number of Test-Takers, and Share of the Pool, 2026.** Cells at 1500 and above are the posterior median with the 95% credible interval in brackets. Cells at 1400 are computed directly from the published band percentages and have no interval. Every value above 1400 is an extrapolation. The pool share is the group's count divided by the total count at or above the threshold, with all eight groups in the denominator. Band percentages and group sizes taken from College Board (2026, pp. 9 and 11). Model values calculated by us from the fitted model.")
```

## Sensitivity Results for All Groups {.unnumbered}

Appendix Table A4 gives, for each of the four fits in @tbl-sens,
every group's share of the pool at or above 1500 and at or above
1580, as a posterior median, with the 95% interval shown for the
canonical fit. As in @tbl-sens, all four fits use the first imputed
dataset, so that interval omits rounding uncertainty and is narrower
than the one in Appendix Table A3.

```{r}
#| label: appendix-a4
#| echo: false
a4_variants <- list(
  `Canonical sinh-arcsinh` = list(sens_ref, "shash"),
  `Two-piece skew-t`       = list(sens_fit$skewt$draws, "skewt"),
  `Wide tail-weight prior` = list(sens_fit$widedelta$draws, "widedelta"),
  `Year-varying skewness`  = list(sens_fit$epsyear$draws, "epsyear"))
a4 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(1500, 1580), function(t) {
  pools <- lapply(a4_variants, function(v) {
    cc <- sapply(seq_along(RACES), function(r)
      SD$N[r, yH] * sens_p_above(v[[1]], v[[2]], t, r))
    100 * cc / rowSums(cc)
  })
  canon <- apply(pools[[1]], 2, function(x) sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", median(x),
                                                    quantile(x, .025), quantile(x, .975)))
  others <- sapply(pools[-1], function(m) apply(m, 2, function(x) sprintf("%.2f", median(x))))
  data.frame(Group = c(sprintf("**At or above %d**", t), RACE_LABEL),
             Canonical = c("", canon), rbind("", others),
             check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
}))
names(a4)[-(1:2)] <- c("Skew-t", "Wide prior", "Year-varying")
kable(a4, align = c("l", rep("r", ncol(a4) - 1)), row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "**Appendix Table A4. Share of the Pool at or above 1500 and 1580 by Group under Alternative Model Specifications, 2026.** Each cell is a posterior median in percent from a single-imputation fit. The canonical sinh-arcsinh column also shows the 95% credible interval in brackets. The other columns are the two-piece skew-t, the five-fold wider tail-weight prior, and year-varying skewness, as in the main-text sensitivity table. Both thresholds lie above the last point checked by group, and 1580 also lies beyond the cohort-level check at 1500. Calculated by us from the fitted models, using data from College Board (2026).")
```
